title: Tipping in Kenya: How Much to Tip on Safari, at Lodges and on Mount Kenya
meta_title: Tipping in Kenya: 7 Simple Rules for Safari Tips
meta_description: Tipping in Kenya made simple: how much to tip safari guides, lodge staff, porters and Mount Kenya crews, in dollars or shillings, plus a 7-day budget.
excerpt: Tipping in Kenya explained by our Nairobi team: realistic amounts for driver-guides, lodge staff, porters and Mount Kenya crews, a worked 7-day tip budget and how to carry the cash.
content:
Tipping in Kenya on safari is customary but never compulsory: plan on about US$10-20 per person per day for your driver-guide, US$5-15 per person per night for the lodge staff tip box, and small amounts for porters and transfers. Tips are paid in cash at the end of each stay.

Most first-time visitors to Kenya worry about tipping too little, tipping too much or getting the etiquette wrong in front of someone they have spent a week with. This guide to tipping in Kenya from our Nairobi team sets out who to tip, realistic amounts in dollars and shillings, a worked budget for a typical safari, Mount Kenya crew tips and how to carry the cash.

Photo: Divulge Adventures

Quick Facts

  • Is tipping expected: Customary on safari, but always optional and linked to the service you received
  • Driver-guide: About US$10-20 per person per day on a shared safari; more for a private vehicle
  • Lodge and camp staff: About US$5-15 per person per night, through the staff tip box
  • Porters and transfers: KSh 100-200 per bag; US$2-10 per transfer depending on length
  • Restaurants: Around 10% if no service charge is already on the bill
  • Currency: Clean, recent US dollars or Kenyan shillings; KSh 129.94 to US$1 on 8 October 2026 (Central Bank of Kenya, checked October 2026)
  • When to tip: At the end of each lodge stay and at the end of the safari, not after every drive

How Much Should You Tip on a Kenya Safari?

A Kenya safari tip usually works out at US$15-35 per person per day once the driver-guide and lodge staff are both covered. The driver-guide takes the largest share because they are with you all day, every day. Everything else is small, occasional amounts for people who carry bags, drive transfers or lead activities.

The figures below are the ranges we see most travellers use and the ones published by most safari camps in East Africa. They are guidelines for tipping in Kenya, not fees. If service was outstanding, give more; if something went wrong and was not put right, it is fine to give less and tell us why so we can fix it.

WhoTypical tipHow it is given
Driver-guide (shared vehicle)US$10-20 per person per dayEnvelope, by hand, on the last day
Driver-guide (private vehicle)About US$20-40 per day for a couple or small family, more for bigger groupsEnvelope, by hand, on the last day
Lodge or camp staffUS$5-15 per person per nightStaff tip box or envelope to the manager at checkout
Camp guide, tracker or spotter (conservancies)US$5-20 per person per dayDirectly, at the end of your stay
Porters and bellboysKSh 100-200 per bag or arrivalDirectly, at the time
Airport or hotel transfer driverUS$2-10 per transferDirectly, on arrival
Restaurants and barsAbout 10% if no service chargeCash on the table or to the waiter

The camp guide, tracker and spotter line mostly applies in private conservancies, where the lodge supplies its own guides and you may not use your Nairobi driver-guide on every drive. In the national reserves and parks, your driver-guide usually does all the game drives.

Tipping in Kenya for Your Driver-Guide

Your driver-guide should get the biggest single tip of the trip: about US$10-20 per person per day on a shared or group safari. The Divulge Adventures Kenya trip pages list tips as not included and give a guideline of about US$10 per person per day, which is a fair base for good service.

Photo: Divulge Adventures

A Kenyan driver-guide does far more than drive. They read animal behaviour to put you in the right place for a crossing or a kill, handle park gates and permits, manage rough roads after rain and often act as your translator, naturalist and problem-solver. For tipping in Kenya, moving towards US$20 per person per day is common when a guide went well beyond the basics.

Shared vehicle or private safari: does the amount change?

On a private safari the tip is often thought of per vehicle rather than per person. A couple in a private 4x4 might give US$20-40 per day between them, while a family of five might give more in total but less per head. On a group departure, tipping in Kenya is individual: each traveller tips separately, and nobody will compare amounts.

When and how should you hand it over?

Give the driver-guide tip once, at the end of the safari, usually at the airport or your Nairobi hotel. Put the cash in an envelope with a short thank-you note; lodges will often give you an envelope if you ask at reception. Handing it over discreetly, with a handshake and a few words of thanks, is the normal way to do it in Kenya.

Tipping Lodge and Camp Staff in Kenya

Lodge and camp staff in Kenya are tipped through a communal staff tip box, usually at reception or in the mess tent, at about US$5-15 per person per night. The money is pooled and shared among the whole team, including the kitchen, housekeeping, security and maintenance staff you rarely see.

Photo: Divulge Adventures

For tipping in Kenya lodges, pay the staff tip once, when you check out, rather than every night. Some camps suggest an amount per room instead of per person; around KSh 2,000 (roughly US$15) per room per night is a common figure for mid-range and upmarket camps. At luxury properties with very high staff-to-guest ratios, guests often tip towards the top of the range. If you are comparing where to stay, our guide to Masai Mara camps by budget explains what each level of camp offers.

Do you tip the manager, a butler or a private guide at the camp?

You do not need to tip the camp manager. If you had a dedicated butler or room attendant, or the camp provided its own guide and tracker on game drives, tip them directly and separately from the staff box. Hand it over on your last morning, after your final activity.

Activities with their own crews

Tipping in Kenya also covers activities with their own staff. Balloon flight crews, ranger-led bush walks, night drives and village visits are all run by people who often appreciate a small tip, typically US$5-10 per person for a half-day activity. Our post on the Masai Mara hot air balloon safari covers what a balloon morning includes, and the Maasai village visits guide explains how village entry fees work, which is separate from any tip.

How Much Does Tipping in Kenya Add to a Safari Budget?

Tipping in Kenya adds roughly US$200-500 per couple to a typical 7-day safari, depending on how generous you are and whether the safari is private. That is a small share of the trip cost, but tipping in Kenya is done in cash you need to carry, so it is worth budgeting before you leave home.

The worked example below is an estimate for two people on a 7-day road safari with 6 nights in lodges or camps. It assumes the low and high ends of the ranges above and is not a Divulge price.

Item (2 people, 7 days)Lower estimateHigher estimate
Driver-guide (US$10-20 per person per day)US$140US$280
Lodge staff boxes (US$5-15 per person per night, 6 nights)US$60US$180
Porters, transfers and activity crewsUS$20US$50
Total estimate per coupleAbout US$220About US$510

Tipping on a Mount Kenya Climb

Tipping on a Mount Kenya climb is shared across the crew and paid by the group. Typical guidance per day is around US$15 for the lead guide, US$10 for an assistant guide, US$10 for the cook and about US$8 for each porter.

Photo: Divulge Adventures

Tipping in Kenya on the mountain adds up because a Mount Kenya crew usually has between three and six people for a small group, more for bigger groups, because porters carry food, tents and equipment between camps. On a 5-day route with a lead guide, cook and three porters, the group tip would work out at roughly US$245 using those figures. Split between four climbers, that is about US$60 each.

Hand over crew tips at the end of the climb, ideally at a short thank-you gathering where each person receives their share directly, so nothing is lost in the middle. Ask your lead guide how many people are on the crew before you set off, so you bring the right amount in small notes. Our 5-Day Mt Kenya Sirimon to Chogoria traverse and the full range of mountain climbing packages list what is included on each trek.

Tipping in Kenya Outside the Safari: Hotels, Restaurants and the Coast

Tipping in Kenya outside the safari is lighter. In Nairobi and coast hotels, give KSh 100-200 to the porter who carries your bags and, if you wish, about KSh 1,000-2,000 per room per day to the staff box at checkout. In restaurants, around 10% is normal where no service charge has been added.

Photo by Ezekiel Kilimo on Unsplash

Is tipping in Kenya expected in restaurants?

Tipping in Kenya restaurants is customary in Nairobi and on the coast, but less so in small local eateries. Always check the bill first: some restaurants already add a service charge, and you do not need to tip twice. If you pay by card, leaving the tip in cash makes it more likely to reach the waiting staff.

Beach hotels, boat trips and day trips

On the coast, dhow and snorkelling crews and beach hotel staff are tipped in the same small amounts as safari activities. For a Nairobi day trip, such as a visit to Nairobi National Park, a tip of around US$10 per person for the driver-guide is reasonable. Our list of day trips from Nairobi covers the options.

What Currency Should You Use for Tipping in Kenya?

US dollars and Kenyan shillings are both fine for tipping in Kenya. Dollars suit larger tips to guides and lodges, while shillings are better for porters and waiters. The Central Bank of Kenya rate was KSh 129.94 to US$1 on 8 October 2026 (checked October 2026), so KSh 1,000 is just under US$8.

Bring clean, recent US dollar notes in small denominations (US$1, US$5, US$10 and US$20). Older, torn or marked notes are often refused, so ask your bank for newer bills. You can check the latest official rate on the Central Bank of Kenya website before you travel, and confirm current amounts with us before you book.

Can you tip by card or M-Pesa?

Remote camps rarely add tips to a card, so plan on cash for tipping in Kenya's parks. M-Pesa, Kenya's mobile money service, is another option: foreign visitors can register a Safaricom line with their passport at a Safaricom shop or M-Pesa agent and send shillings to a guide's phone. It is handy if you run short of cash, but check with the person first.

Keep your money for tipping in Kenya separate from your spending money, and pack it in your hand luggage rather than checked bags. Our Kenya safari packing list covers money belts and what else to carry, and is Kenya safe for safari has practical advice on carrying cash.

Insider Tips

  • Budget before you fly: Work out your total for tipping in Kenya at home and bring it in small, clean notes
  • Use envelopes: Label one per guide and one per lodge so you are not counting cash in front of people
  • Tip at the end: One tip per lodge stay and one for your guide on the last day is the normal pattern
  • Mix currencies: Dollars for the big tips, shillings for porters, waiters and small extras
  • Check the bill: Look for a service charge in restaurants and hotels before adding a tip
  • Say why: A short note naming a great sighting or a kindness means a lot to guides and staff

Frequently Asked Questions

These are the questions travellers ask us most often about tipping in Kenya.

Is tipping in Kenya mandatory on safari?

No, tipping in Kenya is not mandatory, but it is customary on safari and most guides and lodge staff rely on it as part of their income. Treat the usual ranges as a guideline linked to service. If something went wrong and was not fixed, you can tip less, and it helps to tell your safari company so the problem can be put right.

How much should I tip my safari driver-guide in Kenya?

Most travellers tip a Kenya safari driver-guide about US$10-20 per person per day on a shared safari. On a private safari, a couple often gives around US$20-40 per day between them. Give the tip once, at the end of the safari, in an envelope with a short note, and tip more if the guide went well beyond the basics.

Should I tip in US dollars or Kenyan shillings?

Both are accepted for tipping in Kenya. US dollars work well for larger tips to guides and lodge staff, while Kenyan shillings are better for porters, waiters and small extras. Bring clean, recent dollar notes in small denominations, because older, torn or marked notes are often refused. The rate was about KSh 130 to US$1 in October 2026.

How much should I budget for tips on a 7-day Kenya safari?

A couple on a 7-day Kenya safari should budget roughly US$220-510 for tips in total. That covers the driver-guide at US$10-20 per person per day, lodge staff boxes at US$5-15 per person per night, and small amounts for porters, transfers and activity crews. Private safaris and luxury camps tend to sit at the higher end.

How much do you tip on a Mount Kenya climb?

On a Mount Kenya climb, tips are shared across the crew and paid by the whole group. Typical guidance is about US$15 per day for the lead guide, US$10 for an assistant guide, US$10 for the cook and around US$8 for each porter. Hand the tips over at the end of the trek so each crew member receives their share directly.

Final Thoughts

Tipping in Kenya is simple once you know the pattern: about US$10-20 per person per day for your driver-guide, US$5-15 per person per night for lodge staff, and small amounts for everyone else. Budget around US$200-500 per couple for a week and tip at the end of each stay.
